idiom_name: struct { int topic; void (*fn)(void *, const struct event *); void *user_data; } table + publish() loop
implementation_notes: C has no language-level events, so the event channel is an explicit table of subscriber records - a topic or event id, a function pointer and a user-data pointer - that publish() walks and invokes for every match. Registry capacity, removal-while-dispatching and thread safety are all the application's responsibility: dispatch over a snapshot or mark entries for deferred removal, and guard the table with a mutex when publishers and subscribers live on different threads. This manual record is the honest default; only when GLib is already linked does the GObject signal system supply a ready-made channel with reference-counted objects.
pitfalls: Removing a subscriber during dispatch shifts the array under the loop: mark entries dead and compact after the publish pass, or dispatch over a snapshot.
The registry owns no memory: a subscriber that frees its user_data without unsubscribing leaves a dangling pointer that the next publish calls.
Unsynchronised subscribe/publish from different threads corrupts the table; a mutex or a single-threaded channel is mandatory.

variants.name: GObject signal system (GLib)
variants.implementation_notes: When GLib is already a dependency, GObject signals are the C realization of the channel: g_signal_connect(instance, "signal-name::detail", handler, user_data) registers a handler and g_signal_emit() invokes all handlers synchronously before the default handler returns. Emission, detail strings and handler memory management are provided, and object destruction disconnects handlers automatically through the reference-counted object model - at the cost of adopting the GObject type system and its class boilerplate.
pitfalls: g_signal_connect cannot fail: a mistyped signal name only produces a critical warning and the handler is never called, so a silent non-delivery looks like a subscriber bug.
Handlers run synchronously inside g_signal_emit(); a handler that destroys the emitting object continues against freed state, so lifetime rules must be documented per signal.
The user_data pointer follows GObject memory conventions only when the handler is connected with a destroy notify; otherwise it leaks or dangles.
